per_comment.reason: B states the test work as an explicit request ("Add mismatched source and `collection_override` tests"), while A buries it in the hedge "tests would cover this path"; the bullets also separate the guard change from the test as two checkable items.

Two genuinely independent deliverables (retain old files, add a mid-write failure test) are each visible as bullets in A; B's "would cover this path" phrasing makes the test read as optional commentary.
There is one change plus one "no change needed" allowance; A's "can still drive" marks that clearly, whereas B's repeated "Keep… / Keep…" bullets flatten a preservation note into a second work item.

A's verb phrase "atomically replace the report" names actor and action directly; B's "use an atomic report replacement" turns the same instruction into a noun stack at the head of an already long sentence.
The two versions are word-for-word identical, so neither can help the author more.

Only one change is requested; A's "Empty optional cells can remain allowed" reads as the exception it is, while B's imperative bullet "Keep empty optional cells allowed" under a "Requested actions" heading implies a second task.

A's second sentence ("Expected 401 responses can keep their current handling") clearly scopes the fix; B recasts that same exception as a bullet action about a "current handling path," adding template noise for a single change.

The request is one deferral plus an explicit carve-out; A states the carve-out with "can keep the current warning path," while B's second bullet reads as extra work under a "Requested actions" heading.

B splits the constraint into its own sentence ("Unexpected program or infrastructure errors can remain visible"), where A's trailing "while leaving … visible" clause stacks the catch scope and the exclusion into one dense sentence.
The only difference is "once to keep" versus "once, keeping"; both convey the same single action and the same two preserved properties with equal effort.

For one short action plus one exit-code constraint, B's single sentence ("save the shared report for either collection while keeping the nonzero exit conditional on failures") carries everything A needs a heading and two bullets to say.

Three separately checkable items (reject directory-target symlinks, preserve file-symlink behavior, add two kinds of tests) are each visible in A; B compresses them into a "while keeping" clause plus a hedged "would cover the boundary" sentence.

A names the target flag ("Require one or more values for `--models`") and states the no-match check as a requested action; B drops the flag name and softens the second fix to "A no-match check can stop before…".
The two versions are identical in wording and structure.
After the four-part ID recipe, A gives the retrieval-time constraint its own sentence; B's semicolon appends it to an already long enumeration, so the second requirement is easy to miss on one read.

B's "can stay explicit exclusions" tells the author no work is needed for that class, whereas A's parallel bullet under "Requested actions" makes a possibly no-op preservation look like a second task.
Both versions are the same text, including the single "keep both counts visible" request.

The two versions are identical, down to the single mapping-reuse request.

summary: Both versions open with the same strong pattern — a labeled one-line defect statement followed by the triggering condition — so defect clarity is effectively equal, and seven pairs are textually identical. The differences are all in the closing request: an explicit "Requested actions" list wins whenever a test or a second real change would otherwise be softened into "would cover this path", and loses whenever it recasts an exception or a no-op preservation as an imperative bullet. Version A lands on the better side of that split more often, mainly by naming tests as requested work and by keeping carve-outs in modal prose.
